records.name: Kaliningrad
records.current_summary:
No division-specific transgender evidence appears in the surviving sources; a visitor here stands under the national framework as it operates countrywide.

As those sources establish: same-sex activity is not criminalised, but the 2023 laws ban same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition; the 'extremism' designation has produced 101 convictions since early 2024, with 'propaganda' penalties surging to 257 in 2023-24; official asylum guidance singles out trans people, open activists and one conflict-affected region cluster for heightened risk.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (June 2025) is the national framework this division is assessed under: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no division-specific information beyond that national framework.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison; HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3) for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 versus 22 in 2021-22. This national enforcement baseline underlies this division's assessment at the national score; the article contains no division-specific detail.

records.name: Bashkortostan
records.current_summary:
Nothing division-specific appears in the surviving sources; a visitor stands under the national framework as applied countrywide.

As the sources establish: a foreign government's travel advisory warns that 'propaganda'-law convictions can bring arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation for foreigners, and that displaying rainbow symbols is itself criminal; the 2023 laws ban legal gender recognition; the extremism designation has produced 101 convictions since early 2024.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025; updated 12 August 2026) is the national framework this division is assessed under: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned; the 'gay propaganda' law makes public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition — including displaying rainbow symbols — punishable by fines up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and repeated offences can bring up to four years' imprisonment; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023; the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023, and between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws. No division-specific information about Bashkortostan appears.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (blocked by the site's security service); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for this country: advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics, warns that foreigners found guilty under the 'propaganda' law may be arrested, detained up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison; HRW also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses) for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media; the 2013 'gay propaganda' law already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence. National enforcement baseline with no division-specific detail for Bashkortostan.

records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.
records.current_outOfScope: Province-level violent-crime and gender-based-violence rates run above the national baseline; this is ordinary-crime context and does not move trans-specific risk (none of the reporting identifies trans victims).

sources.claim: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

sources.title: LGBT rights in South Africa - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national dossier this Free State record is assessed under: the 1996 Constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination, the Constitutional Court's December 2005 judgment pushed Parliament to legalise same-sex marriage (Civil Union Act, National Assembly vote 229-41, November 2006), and the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act 2003 allows a person to change sex status in the population registry - and therefore on identity documents and passports - on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The page adds that gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like the Free State 'must travel long distances to major cities' to reach it, with private treatment costing hundreds of thousands of rands and long public waiting lists, and records the Justice Department's National Task Team (2011) and 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities aimed at hate crimes against LGBT people. This grounds the record's at-national-score assessment in the concrete national framework a Free State visitor stands under, since no Free State-specific trans source was surfaced.

freshness_all.fact: Mokoena judgment strengthened trans-inmate rights (DCS ordered to afford gender expression + state-funded HRT), but it is a Gauteng/Johannesburg Centre case - misattributed to a Free State record; DCS national policy is the correct frame.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018) on transgender women in French prisons: under Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code men and women are held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, without sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities; a detainee recalled inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' and threats of violence; Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, says transgender detainees — overwhelmingly women — are the group that suffers the most in prison, illustrated by American trans woman Kara B. held in 'worrying' conditions. National prison-placement framework; no division-specific detail for this region.

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010): it records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres; the review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. National custodial-inspection framework; no division-specific finding for this region.

records.name: Normandie
records.current_summary:
No division-specific transgender findings appear in the surviving sources; the national mechanisms they document apply here unchanged.

In short: prison placement follows the legal sex on identity documents (Criminal Procedure Code art. D248), so trans women are typically housed in men's facilities; the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons and names them the group that suffers most in custody.
